**Helping Your Child Succeed in Maths: Why We're Changing How We Teach**

---

**What's changing?**

From September, your child will be in a mixed-ability maths class instead of a "top," "middle," or "bottom" set.

---

**Why we're making this change**

**The old way wasn't working for enough children**

Research shows that streaming often hurts more students than it helps:

- **Students in lower sets tend to stay there** — even when they could do better. Teachers sometimes expect less, and students start to expect less of themselves.
- **Being in a lower set affects confidence** — children often believe they "can't do maths," which becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy.
- **Students in top sets can feel intense pressure** — and may develop gaps in understanding because the pace moves too fast for deep learning.
- **Many students are simply in the wrong set** — a bad test day, a difficult year, or even behaviour issues can place a capable student in a lower stream.

**Mixed-ability teaching helps more children succeed**

- **Students learn from each other** — explaining your thinking to someone else is one of the best ways to understand something deeply.
- **Teachers plan more carefully** — they must think about different ways to explain concepts, which benefits everyone.
- **No child is labelled as "good" or "bad" at maths** — this protects confidence and keeps options open for the future.
- **Students see different approaches to problems** — this builds flexible thinking, which is what maths in the real world requires.

---

**"But I was in the bottom set and it was fine" or "I was in the top set and I needed it"**

We understand these feelings. Many of us had the same experience. But "fine" or "surviving" isn't our goal — we want every child to thrive.

Being in a top set doesn't guarantee deep understanding. Being in a lower set often closes doors to higher qualifications, regardless of actual potential.

---

**"Won't the bright children be held back?"**

No. Research shows that high-attaining students do just as well — and often better — in mixed classes. They develop stronger reasoning skills by explaining their thinking and tackling more open-ended problems.

Teachers will still provide challenges at different levels within the same classroom. The difference is that students can move between levels of challenge as needed, rather than being fixed in one group.

---

**"My child needs to be with students at the same level"**

Children are rarely at the "same level" in all areas of maths. Your child might be confident with fractions but struggle with shapes. Mixed-ability grouping allows them to work at the right level for each topic.

---

**"How will the teacher manage a whole class with different needs?"**

Teachers use strategies like:

- **Same task, different depths** — everyone works on the same problem, but with different levels of support or extension
- **Careful grouping within lessons** — sometimes students work in similar-ability pairs, sometimes mixed
- **Regular checks on understanding** — so no one falls behind unnoticed

Our teachers are receiving training in these methods.

---

**What this means for your child**

- They will be in a class with a full range of students
- They will sometimes work independently, sometimes in pairs or groups
- They will be encouraged to talk about their thinking and try different approaches
- They will have access to the full maths curriculum, keeping all future options open

---

**What you can do to help**

- **Avoid saying "I was never good at maths"** — this gives children permission to give up
- **Ask "How did you work that out?"** rather than just "Did you get it right?"
- **Praise effort and thinking** — not just speed or correct answers
- **Trust the process** — change takes time, and we will monitor how your child is doing

---

**Questions?**

We know this is a significant change. Please contact [name/role] on [contact details] if you would like to discuss your child's situation specifically.

We are making this change because we believe every child deserves the chance to succeed in mathematics — not just those who were lucky enough to be placed in the right set.

---

*This decision is based on research from the Education Endowment Foundation, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, and decades of studies on mathematics teaching.*
